p: The seal passed its fifteen year aging test, and HEARTH held air through proof at a third of its allowed leak.
Commander Tess Okonjo took bunk four for the crew evaluation, and in the night fire run the smoke pooled behind her curtain while the cabin sensor Nadia had verified never went off.
A detector is going in at the head of every bunk, and at the test readiness review Nadia reopened her own fire detection row in red.
Everything else is cleared to test, but fire detection holds until every quarter is proven at the pillow.
Callie and Nadia are talking again, and her father asked her to leave Tess's photo of her two boys up when she tests it.
Helen Cho-Ramirez. Halo's crew lead. She passed on that Tess is keeping four.
Gus. Test cell technician. He put the flight harness back in.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. He watched proof with his hand on the glass.
Amara Osei. Program manager. She held fire detection at the review.
Tiago Ferreira. Test lead. He told Nadia nobody sleeps at the detector.
Ken Mallory. Halo's program manager. He signs for HEARTH on the dock.
Ines. Quality manager. She wrote the root cause into verification planning.
Tess Okonjo. Halo's commander. She sleeps in four, her boys' photo up.

The detectors came up from Halo on Wednesday of week thirty four in a gray case, foam cut for six and four of the holes filled. Each one was about the size of a hockey puck. They were Halo's own spares, the station's standard unit, and the shelf they'd come off was empty now.

Gus mounted them Thursday, one at the head of each bunk, right where the particle counters had hung for the crew run. Jun wired each one into HEARTH's caution and warning, so smoke in any quarter would set off the station's tones through the whole module. Odette rewrote the detection control in the fire hazard report around them that night. She kept the cabin sensor in it. It still watched the galley, and the galley was still worth watching.

The plan was Nadia's, and it was long. Eight places a fire could start: the galley, the fan behind the hygiene panel, the rack bay, the power distribution unit, and the reading light in each quarter. Every curtain shut. Lights out. Each source with both cabin fans running, then again with one switched off, and the duct fan in the aft hatch pushing node air the whole time. Sixteen runs a night, two nights. Every detector timed from the first wisp, and a counter at every pillow to show how thick it got there before anything went off.
Ines stood at the console with the procedure and initialed each run. Helen flew in for the second night and pulled a chair in beside her.

Tess's photo was still on the wall in four. Nobody had taken it down. Ines had put it on the configuration list herself, one line under the ground plugs: photograph, two boys and a fish, Scotch tape, ground item, remove before flight. Nadia left it up.

The last run was Helen's own scenario from the crew evaluation. Sleep period, the source behind the hygiene panel, one fan off. Nadia asked to take bunk four herself. Odette said fine, as long as Nadia held a stop button too, and Helen dug a pair of orange foam earplugs out of her coat pocket and handed them over without a word. They were the kind the last one out had worn, nine years ago, behind his shut door.

Behind the curtain it was dark and close and smelled faintly of new foam. The boys were a hand from her face, holding up their fish. She counted the way Jun's stopwatch would. Somewhere past twenty she could smell it, sweet and faint, like the dance in the high school gym. At forty one the tones went, loud enough through the earplugs to sit her straight up, and the detector over her head was flashing white across the photo.
Forty one, Helen said over the speaker, like she was reading it off a sticky note.

It was the slowest of the thirty two runs. The requirement said sixty. Jun checked his model against both nights, then ran the same case with gravity off, as it would be on orbit, and got forty seven. Ines signed the record at ten past two in the morning. Fire detection, verified by test at the head of each bunk, with analysis for orbit. N. Brooks.

In the lot she sent her father a picture: the detector on the wall, and next to it two boys and one small fish. She didn't expect anything back till morning. It came at ten after five, when he'd have been on his first cup.
A text from Dad. GOOD. NOW GO HOME AND SLEEP IN YOURS.
Colleen's Flight Notes: the long tail.

On Saturday of week thirty six a flatbed backed up to the hangar door at the air museum at old Lowry with a retired trainer jet on it, the wings off and strapped down alongside. Colleen had given the museum her Saturdays for years. She handed Nadia one end of a clipboard.
Nobody signs till we've walked it, she said. It sat in a desert yard twenty years. I want to know what the ride did to it.

Transition moves a system into the place it will work and hands it over, able to do its job, to the people who'll run and support it. It's planned early, with whoever receives it, and the plan covers far more than the trip. It covers the enabling systems for packaging, handling, storage and transport, the site and the installation, the training, the spares and data, and the checks at the far end. When the system arrives it's installed and checked out in place, to confirm it survived the trip and works where it now lives. Operators and maintainers are trained, records change hands, and the receiver confirms it's ready for operation. A readiness review before it ships asks whether the system and everything going with it are ready to move, against criteria agreed with the receiver. Some risks travel with it, too. Launch insurance transfers the cost of losing a spacecraft to an insurer. It doesn't make the launch any safer.

Here's the card for transition. Its purpose is to establish the system's capability to provide its services in the operational environment, and hand it to the people who'll run and support it. It takes in the verified system, the transition strategy agreed with the receiver, the enabling systems for packing, moving and installing it, and the training material. It puts out the system installed and checked out where it will work, trained operators and maintainers, the handover records, and any anomalies found on the way. Operation takes it from there, and maintenance takes over its support.

When a new system replaces an old one that's still working, transition plans the cutover. In a parallel run, both work side by side for a while and their results are compared, with the old one kept as a fallback. In a phased switch, one site or one function moves at a time. A single switch overnight needs a tested way back if the new system fails. Transition is done when the receiving organization accepts the system for use, not when the truck leaves.

How the exam asks it. Transition: planned early with the receiver, enabling systems for the move, install and check out at the destination, train, hand over records, confirm ready. Operation takes the installed system next. Insurance is risk transfer. Cutover can be a parallel run, a phased switch or a single switch with a way back, and transition ends when the receiver accepts the system.

The jet's logbooks came in a banker's box: thirty four years of who flew it, who fixed it, and what came off it and why. Colleen turned pages with one finger. This one ate starters, she said. Four in two years. Then somebody changed the ground cart and it quit. The book knew before anybody did.

Operation uses the system to deliver its services. It readies trained operators, procedures and the support they need, runs the system, watches how it performs, and records anomalies and passes them on. Maintenance keeps the system able to deliver. Corrective maintenance fixes failures. Preventive maintenance acts before they happen, on a schedule or on what monitoring shows. Adaptive and perfective maintenance change the system to fit new conditions or to work better. Logistics keeps maintenance supplied: spares sized from reliability and maintainability data and placed where they'll be needed, supply, packaging, handling, storage and transport, tools and training. Parts go out of production, so obsolescence gets planned too, sometimes with a lifetime buy. Maintenance records send failure data back to the engineers. Utilization and Support run side by side, and logistics is one of the handbook's quality characteristics because support has to be designed in along with the system.

Here's the card for operation. Its purpose is to use the system to deliver its services. It takes in the installed system, its operating procedures, trained operators, and the support they need. It puts out the services the system exists for, performance data, anomaly and incident reports, and help for users who run into trouble. Maintenance takes the anomaly reports next, and the engineers take the performance data to improve the system.

Here's the card for maintenance. Its purpose is to sustain the system's capability to provide its services. It takes in the failure and anomaly reports, its maintenance strategy and procedures, and the spares and tools logistics supplies. It puts out a restored system, maintenance records and failure data. The engineers use that data next to update reliability estimates, spares and sometimes the design, and logistics uses it to restock.

A few duties sit inside those two cards. Operation keeps contingency procedures ready to keep or restore service when something fails, and it keeps every operator trained and current, including the ones who joined after the first class. Maintenance reads its records across every unit and every mission, not one at a time, because a repeat failure only shows up when you look at all of them together.

Maintenance is planned in levels. Some work happens where the system lives, done by its own operators with the tools at hand. Some happens at a shop with more tools and skill. Some only the maker can do. On orbit, the first level is the crew with what's aboard. Anything bigger waits for a cargo flight or doesn't happen at all, which is why the design settles so much of it.

Support can be run as a service. The customer buys an outcome, like an anomaly answered within an agreed time, rather than hours of engineering. Service systems engineering designs the people, processes and tools that deliver it, agrees service levels with the customer, and measures them in use, which is where a service's value shows up.

A system in service also changes. A modification during operation runs through the same processes again, needs, requirements, design, verification, transition, as a small life cycle inside the big one, with configuration management keeping the record of which unit has which change.

How the exam asks it. Operation uses the system and watches it. Maintenance sustains it: corrective, adaptive, perfective and preventive actions (condition based is a kind of preventive), plus logistics. Spares come from reliability data, and failure data from maintenance goes back to engineering. A service is judged on agreed outcomes.

Before the jet came inside, Colleen showed Nadia the yard's work order. Fuel drained. Fluids drained. Ejection seat charges pulled and destroyed. Radios out, batteries gone. It's a museum piece because somebody planned it that way, she said. Otherwise it's a hazard with a nice paint job.

Disposal ends a system's existence for its intended use. It also handles the elements removed or replaced during its life, and whatever special disposal needs were identified, from hazardous materials to data. It starts in the concept stage, because design decides what can be taken apart safely, recycled, or brought down from orbit. When the time comes it deactivates the system, takes it out of service, dismantles or destroys it as planned, keeps retired parts from finding their way back into use, deals with the hazards, and leaves the environment as it should be. Then it confirms nothing harmful was left behind, and the records are archived in a form someone can still read. For a spacecraft, the plan covers making it safe by removing stored energy, called passivation, and bringing it out of orbit, usually in a controlled reentry over empty ocean, with an analysis of which parts might survive.

Here's the card for disposal. Its purpose is to take a system or element out of its intended use, deal with what's replaced or retired, and meet any special disposal needs. It takes in the disposal strategy, planned since concept, the retired system or elements, and the limits set by law and the environment. It puts out a system taken out of service, a site or an orbit left as it should be, records of what was done, and archived records. Knowledge management takes the lessons, and the archive keeps the records for as long as the rules require. Data gets the same care as hardware. Stored data is wiped or destroyed so nobody can recover it, unless the records rules say it has to be kept.
Environmental impact runs all the way through it as part of sustainability, because what a system leaves behind counts as much as what it did.

How the exam asks it. Disposal is planned from the concept stage. It covers retired elements during the life too. Prevent reuse, handle hazards, confirm, archive. Sustainability counts what's left behind.

The restoration crew ate lunch on folding chairs in the hangar. A retired crew chief in his seventies ran the floor. The museum's director, who ran the money and the opening date, sat beside him and argued with him about both, and a high school junior in a borrowed coverall sat at his other elbow writing down everything he said. She runs the date and the dollars, Colleen said, tipping her head at the director. He tells her what's true about the airplane. Neither of them gets to stop listening.

The handbook's last part is about doing systems engineering among people. Systems engineering and project management overlap and lean on each other. The project manager owns the project as a business: cost, schedule, resources, the agreement and the customer relationship. The systems engineer owns the technical whole: needs and requirements, architecture, the technical baseline, how the disciplines fit together, and the technical side of risk and decisions. Planning, risk, reviews and change are shared ground, and programs go best when the two work it together instead of guarding the line. Systems engineers often lead without line authority, by keeping the whole in view and asking the questions no single discipline owns.

The same overlap runs with software and hardware engineering, and the two move at different speeds. Software now carries much of what most systems do. It's cheap to change, so software teams tend to work in short increments and keep changing it after delivery. It doesn't wear out, but its faults can sit hidden until the right conditions reach them. Hardware has long lead times, physical limits like mass, power and heat, and a real price on every change once parts are made, so its decisions settle earlier. Systems engineering works across both. It brings software and hardware people into the architecture from the start, so which function goes where is a trade, not a habit. It hands each of them the frame they work inside: the requirements allocated to their part, the interfaces between parts, and the plan for putting the parts together and checking them. It plans around the speed gap too, with simulators and early boards so software can be tested before the real hardware exists. And it keeps watch on the seams where the two meet, since that's where late surprises tend to hide. The disciplines design and build the elements, and what they learn as they go comes back into the architecture.

Culture decides how much of that works. A team that makes it safe to raise a problem early, and treats disagreement as information, finds trouble while it's still cheap. The handbook counts diversity, equity and inclusion as part of that: people with different backgrounds see different parts of a problem, if the team makes room for every one of them to be heard.

Teams do better with a few plain habits. They share practices and one current source of information, so nobody works from a stale copy. When a team spans companies or time zones, an agreed glossary saves weeks of people using the same word for different things. Integrated product teams put design, manufacturing, test and support people on one element from the start. And a leader who criticizes every reported mistake teaches people to hide them, until they're expensive.

Technical leadership is one of the competencies the handbook names, and most of it happens without a title. It means holding a technical vision people can follow, explaining it to engineers and to people who aren't, making hard calls and saying why, and building the team that does the work. A systems engineer who needs a discipline lead to change a design makes the case with the shared goal and the evidence, not with rank. Explaining a technical risk to company leaders starts with what it means for their goals, and then the evidence behind it.

Systems engineers also work beside the specialty engineers: safety, reliability, human factors, security, logistics and the rest. Each brings deep knowledge of one property of the whole. The systems engineer's job is to bring them in early, give them the architecture and the scenarios to work from, and fold what they find into one design, so no specialty's answer surprises the others late.

The competency framework sorts what systems engineers need into five groups. Core covers the basics everyone needs, like systems thinking, life cycles and modeling. Professional covers how they work with people: communication, ethics, technical leadership, negotiation, team skills and coaching. Technical covers the life cycle processes themselves, from requirements to operation. Management covers planning, assessment, decisions, risk, configuration and information. Integrating covers the neighboring fields an engineer has to work with, such as project management, finance, logistics and quality. Each competency is rated at five levels: awareness, supervised practitioner, practitioner, lead practitioner and expert. People move up through practice, mentoring, training and certification. INCOSE's own certifications follow a ladder too: the associate level this exam leads to, then the certified professional, then the expert, each asking for more documented experience.

Ethics runs under all of it. INCOSE's code of ethics is worth knowing in outline. It starts from a few principles: honesty and integrity, objectivity, and putting the safety, health and welfare of the public first. Then it sets out duties to society and the public, and rules for practice that cover employers, clients and the profession. In practice that means reporting what's true even when nobody wants to hear it, disclosing a conflict of interest and stepping back from any decision it could bend, doing only work you're competent to do and doing it with care, keeping confidences, and speaking up when a decision puts people at risk.

How the exam asks it. PM owns the business side and SE the technical whole, and they share planning, risk, reviews and change. SEs often lead by influence. A culture that welcomes bad news early finds trouble cheaply. The competency framework has five groups, core, professional, technical, management and integrating, rated awareness, supervised practitioner, practitioner, lead practitioner and expert. The code of ethics puts honesty, objectivity and public safety first, with conflicts disclosed and competent, diligent service.

By the cockpit ladder, a placard said the type had been built in eleven versions over twenty two years. Same wing. Mostly the same cockpit. Different engines, different jobs. They didn't design eleven airplanes, Colleen said. They designed one, eleven ways.

Product line engineering builds a family of related systems from one shared set of assets: requirements, architecture, designs, models, test procedures and documents, with the differences between products planned and managed as variation points. The shared assets are engineered and controlled once, and each product is built from them. It costs more up front and pays back with every product after. Copying a design and changing the copy, often called clone and own, is quick for the second product and costly by the fifth, because each copy drifts on its own. Portfolio management decides which projects an organization starts, keeps, redirects or ends, so the whole set fits its strategy and capacity, and gives each its resources.

Product lines need their own discipline. The shared assets are engineered and controlled once, under configuration management, and every variation point says which choices exist and which combinations are allowed. A change to a shared asset ripples to every product built from it, so its impact assessment covers the whole family. Knowledge management turns what one project learned into assets the next one can reuse.

Here's the card for life cycle model management. Its purpose is to define, maintain and make available the policies, life cycle processes, life cycle models and procedures the organization's projects use, and to keep improving them. It takes in the organization's strategy, standards such as 15288, and assessments and lessons from projects. It puts out the organization's processes, models, policies and procedures, the tailoring guidance that goes with them, and improvement actions. Project planning uses them next, tailoring them to each new project.

Improvement runs on evidence. The organization assesses how its processes really perform on projects, compares them with standards and with what better organizations do, and changes them on purpose, under the same kind of control a design gets. A process nobody follows isn't fixed by printing it again. It's fixed by finding out why people work around it.

The last part of the handbook also looks at where the work is heading. Digital engineering puts models and data at the center of every stage, with one authoritative source and tools that talk to each other, and more of the checking done by machines on that data. None of the processes in this book go away. They get faster, and the record gets harder to lose. The judgment stays with people.

They had the wings back on by three. Walking out, Colleen asked about the pre-ship review, and Nadia said she thought they'd be ready. Colleen didn't tell her a gate was where you're allowed to say we're not ready. She'd said that once, over pie. It's also where you get to say ready, she said. People forget that half. If it's true, say it plain.

How the exam asks it. Product line: shared assets, managed variation, not clone and own. Portfolio: the set of projects against strategy and capacity. Life cycle model management: establish, assess, improve processes. Knowledge management: reusable knowledge assets.
Decision one. A crate and a truck.

Tuesday of week thirty three, the week before the detectors came, Wes wrote SHIP on the HEARTH room whiteboard, and under it Friday of week thirty eight, and underlined it twice. The integrated acceptance test had started the afternoon before, with fire detection held out of it until the detectors came. After that HEARTH would wait at the launch site for its rocket, under purge, checked every quarter. Halo wanted it there and ready the day the rocket was.

Halo's launch site team had sent forty questions that morning. What lifting fixture. What the container held for temperature and humidity. Who would train their technicians. Which spares came with the module, and which data. Who would check it when it got there, and against what.
Gus, the test cell technician, read the first ten over Nadia's shoulder. Eleven cargo modules left here in a crate on a truck at night, he said. The crate's already built. What's left to plan?
Halo's launch site team has sent questions on fixtures, storage, training, spares and checkout. What should FRO do?
A. Turn the forty questions into a transition plan agreed with Halo's launch site.
B. Let Halo's launch site team write its own receiving plan from FRO's full drawings.
C. Leave transition planning for the pre-ship review once the configuration is set.
D. Ship it the way the cargo modules went, with Halo's questions answered as they come.

Jun and Tiago turn the forty questions into a plan the launch site signs. The container gets a dry nitrogen purge and recorders for temperature, humidity and shock. The lifting fixture goes with its load test certificate and handling procedures. Two FRO technicians travel. Manuals, spares and the data package go in the plan by name, and so does a checkout at the launch site, run by FRO and Halo together, that repeats the leak and power checks after the trip.

That's the one. The transition process plans, with the receiver, how the system moves to its operational environment: the enabling systems for packaging, handling, storage and transport, installation, training, data, and the checkout that confirms it arrived ready.

Monday of week thirty four Helen brought Halo's lead flight controller to the high bay. For fifteen years HEARTH would be flown from Halo's control center: power, air, heat, alarms, by people who'd never stood in this building. He walked the module with a notebook and asked good questions, mostly about what the rack did when it was unhappy. On the way out he stopped at quarter four and looked at the spot over the pillow where the new detector would go. I'm the one who woke them, he said. The night with the sensor. Helen tells it better. He'd be on console at three in the morning, deciding whether a number on his screen was worth waking four people.
Back in the HEARTH room he closed the notebook and asked FRO to send the procedures and the drawings. His people read fast, he said.
For fifteen years, Halo's control center will fly HEARTH. How should its controllers be prepared?
A. Train his people on HEARTH's real procedures in Jun's model, fault by fault.
B. Send the procedures and drawings, with FRO's engineers on Halo's console for a month.
C. Let Halo's controllers learn HEARTH from the manuals, as the people flying it.
D. Have FRO fly HEARTH from Centennial for fifteen years under the sustaining option.

Nadia offers him a trainer instead. Jun brings the model up to the as-built module and it becomes one. Halo's controllers fly HEARTH's real procedures on it, fault by fault, until the rack's moods are familiar. They agree what Halo watches every shift, which numbers count as healthy, and how an anomaly reaches FRO under the sustaining option, with an engineer on call by name. The model keeps the job for fifteen years, the digital twin where every procedure change gets tried first.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Operation prepares trained operators and procedures, runs the system, monitors its performance, and records and passes on anomalies. A model kept in step with the real system makes a good trainer and test bed.
Decision three. Six and a half fans.
Thursday Pavel, Tamarack's account lead, drove down from Frederick with Irena, and they spread Tamarack's parts list across the HEARTH room table.

Amara was pricing Halo's sustaining option: cost plus fixed fee, fifteen years. The rack's fans were rated at twenty thousand hours between failures. Running every hour for fifteen years, each fan would fail about six and a half times. The controller card's processor was going out of production next year. And Halo's spare detectors had all just gone into HEARTH.
Tamarack will sell you spares whenever you need them, Pavel said. Order one when one breaks.
Each rack fan will likely fail six or seven times in fifteen years. How should FRO plan spares?
A. Leave spares to Halo, who owns the module and its parts after acceptance.
B. Size and place spares from reliability data, with a lifetime buy of the card.
C. Order spares as parts fail, and make a lifetime buy of the controller card now.
D. Stock two of every part on orbit with the crew for the full fifteen years.

Jun's numbers set the spares: enough fans to cover the six and a half failures each with margin for a late cargo flight, some on orbit and the rest on the ground, riding cargo at Halo's cadence. Tamarack builds a lifetime supply of controller cards before the processor ends. Failed fans come home for repair and their records come to FRO. The detectors join Halo's own spares pool, so the station keeps one kind. Amara writes the sustaining option as a service: an answer to any anomaly within four hours, the rack's availability measured every month.

Exactly right. Maintenance includes logistics support: spares sized from reliability and maintainability data and placed where they're needed, supply and transport, planned obsolescence buys, repair, and records that feed failures back to engineering.
Monday of week thirty five Osprey's letter came: FRO had won its habitat module. A little shorter than HEARTH, three quarters instead of four, berthing to a smaller station in two years.

Osprey's engineers had already asked why HEARTH had an aft hatch, and Jun had sent the trade record from week ten: the criteria, the weights, the sensitivity check. They could run it against their own station in an afternoon.
Wes had printed HEARTH's drawing tree and taped it in a strip down the hallway wall. Copy the tree, change what's different, he said. That's how we built cargo eleven times.
A second habitat with three quarters instead of four is on the table. How should FRO approach its design?
A. Design the second module fresh, made for its own station from the very first sketch.
B. Build both from one controlled set of shared parts, with the differences planned.
C. Copy HEARTH's tree for the new module, keeping both in step by hand.
D. Offer the new customer HEARTH exactly as built, with all four of its quarters.

Jun and Wes sort the tree into what both share and what differs. Shared: the ring frames, the hatch that's now built three times, the berthing ring, the rack interface, the model, the test procedures. Different: length, quarters, the host station's power and data. The shared set gets its own baseline and its own board. A change to the hatch is made once and flows to both. Wes takes his tape down, and keeps the printout.

That's the one. Product line engineering builds related products from a shared, controlled set of assets, with the differences planned and managed as variation points, so reuse is designed in rather than copied.
Decision five. Three asks, one cell.

Thursday of week thirty five the board met in the conference room over the lobby, and this time the chair asked for Nadia by name. Three things were on the screen. The second module. Halo's sustaining option, fifteen years and a team of eight to start. And a call from the cargo customer FRO had grown up on, wanting two more cargo modules soon.
All three needed some of the same things: the test cell, the high bay, Wes, Tiago.
Ms. Brooks, the chair said. In the spring I asked whether we could build two of these at once. Now I'm asking about three.
Three asks compete for the same cell, high bay, Wes and Tiago. What should Nadia recommend?
A. Leave the three program managers to share out the cell and the people.
B. Take all three on at once, with the revenue and the jobs they bring.
C. Rank the three by near term revenue, then fund them from the top down.
D. Weigh all three against strategy and capacity, then set their start order.

Nadia and Amara lay the three over the cell's calendar and the people. Sustaining starts now with eight people and barely needs the cell. The second module needs it in its second year. The cargo modules fit the gaps if the customer takes a later start, and the customer does. The plan puts all three in that order, with a review every quarter and one line saying which gives way if the cell runs short. The chair reads that line twice. That's the line my father's company never wrote down, she says, and calls the vote. All three pass.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Portfolio management starts, sustains, redirects or ends projects so the set fits the organization's strategy and capacity. It sets priorities and allocates shared resources, and keeps reviewing the balance.
Friday of week thirty five Halo's disposal planner came to the HEARTH room with a laptop and a short list. She was new to everyone at FRO.

At the end of its life Halo would bring the whole station down at once, in one controlled reentry over the emptiest stretch of the South Pacific, and HEARTH would go down with it. She needed three things from FRO: what in HEARTH might survive reentry, what had to be made safe before the last crew left, and who would still be able to read HEARTH's drawings in fifteen years.

Before anyone answered she told them why she cared about the first one. She'd spent six years on a survey ship in the South Pacific before she came to Halo, and the emptiest water on the chart had never been empty. One night a warning came over the radio about a spent booster coming down, and they moved twenty miles, and it came down close to where they'd been. Whatever survived reentry, she said, was what landed on somebody. She'd like to know which pieces those were while the drawings still had names on them.
That's fifteen years off, Amara said, not unkindly. Does it have to be this week?
The disposal planner asks what survives reentry, what's made safe, and who'll read the drawings. What should FRO do?
A. Leave HEARTH's disposal to Halo, as part of its plan for the station's reentry.
B. Send her the materials list now, with the disposal steps written near end of life.
C. Design in an undock and boost to a higher orbit at end of life instead.
D. Plan HEARTH's disposal with her now, down to the records kept to the end.

Jun runs the materials list for her survival analysis: most of the aluminum shell burns away, and the steel berthing bolts and the titanium hatch hinges might reach the water. HEARTH's end of life steps go into its procedures now. First line, crew items out. Nadia thinks of a photo with Scotch tape on it, and doesn't say so. Then the sorbent beds and batteries made safe, power off at the isolation points, fluid lines isolated. The information plan keeps the drawings and as-built record readable until the day it comes down, in formats picked for that.

Exactly right. Disposal is planned early and designed in: what survives, how the system is made safe and taken out of service, and records kept for the whole life. It's agreed with the stakeholders who'll carry it out.

Tuesday of week thirty six the launch provider's payload integration manager called from the coast. He was building the final loads analysis for the flight, and the trajectory behind it, and he needed HEARTH's mass, its center of gravity, and its moments of inertia.
He had the CDR prediction already, 14,140 kilograms with its growth allowance, and his last loads cycle had used it.
Tiago had the weigh on the schedule for Wednesday: three load cells under the lifting fixture, two days with the setup.
FRO's numbers had tracked close all year, the integration manager said, and he asked whether he really had to wait on a scale.
Tiago has three load cells booked under the lifting fixture for Wednesday. What should the launch provider get?
A. Send him the figures from Halo's monthly chart, as the launch customer.
B. Send him the weighed mass, with center of gravity and inertia from the model.
C. Weigh it as it flies for mass and center of gravity, with the uncertainty stated.
D. Send the CDR prediction, with its growth allowance and a year of close tracking.

Nadia tells him to wait for the scale. Wednesday HEARTH hangs from the fixture over three load cells in flight configuration, ground plugs out, spares stowed as they'll fly. The three readings give the mass and where its center sits across the base. Jun's model supplies the height of the center and the inertia, checked against the weigh. The package goes to the coast that night: the numbers with their uncertainty, what was aboard and what wasn't, and the payload interface document's requirements line by line with the evidence for each.

That's the one. Transition hands the receiver what it needs to integrate the system: measured properties of the delivered configuration, with uncertainty, and evidence the interface requirements are met.
Decision eight. What's left on the floor.

Friday of week thirty six the acceptance test ended, and Tiago walked Nadia around what was left on the high bay floor. The stand-in rack, steel ballast with Tamarack's connectors still on its back. The stand-in's harness set, yellow tape at both ends, built from cargo wire. The forward hatch qualification article on its stand. The seal fixture. Two pallets of foam and strapping.
Scrap pile out back, same as always, Tiago said. The second module wants this floor. Do I call the recycler?
Stand-ins, the qualification hatch and the seal fixture are left on the floor. What should happen to them?
A. Recycle all of it, and log every item by its serial number on the way out the door.
B. Keep all of it at the back of the high bay for the second module to use.
C. Put it all on the scrap pile out back, the way FRO has always handled test hardware.
D. Give each item its own disposition, with anything kept marked as not for flight.

Nadia goes down the floor with Tiago one item at a time. The qualification hatch stays as the second module's fit check article, with a red band painted round it and NOT FOR FLIGHT stenciled on the frame. The stand-in's connectors go to the next stand-in and its ballast back to steel stock. The stand-in's harnesses get cut into lengths no one could ever install, and the shop logs it by serial. Gus asks to do the cutting himself. He starts with the power harness that ran the rack for nine days, and reads each serial out to the shop lead before it goes in the bin. The fixture goes into storage with its records. What's left goes to the recycler, and the hazardous waste contractor takes the rest.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Disposal covers elements retired along the way, not only the system at its end. Each gets a planned disposition, retired parts are kept from coming back into use, hazards are handled, and the records show what happened to each.

Monday of week thirty seven Amara ran the pre-ship review in the big conference room off the lobby. The weigh had come in at 14,218 kilograms in flight configuration, 782 under the allocation, within twenty kilograms of Jun's prediction.
The actions from the test readiness review had closed one at a time, each with its owner's name beside it. The last one was a torn label, the Friday before.

Odette's phase three safety review had closed the last hazard report the week before, the fire one, on the bunk test. Three items were still open. The galley table's new latch, whose parts wouldn't come until the week after ship. A handling redline for the launch site. And a scuff on the aft ring's protective cover.
Ken Mallory, Halo's program manager, had his calendar open. Ship Friday, he said. Whatever's open rides along with it.
Three items are still open at the pre-ship review, including the galley table's new latch. What should Nadia do?
A. Let Halo decide what it accepts at the launch site, after receiving inspection.
B. Set the ship criteria with Halo, then name an owner for each item that travels.
C. Hold the ship until every open item is closed, the galley latch included.
D. Ship Friday with all three open, to be finished at the launch site.

The criteria go on the screen first: verification closed or dispositioned, hazard reports closed at phase three, configuration audited against the as-built list, data package and transition items ready, and every open item with an owner and Halo's agreement. The latch travels, to be installed and verified by FRO's technicians at the launch site. So do the redline and the scuff. Mallory initials all three. Amara asks the room. Nadia reads down the criteria once more, all five, and doesn't nod. Ready, she says. The latch is mine. It rides with us, and I check it myself at the launch site before anybody signs for it. Mallory looks at her for a second, then writes her name beside the latch. Down the table Wes takes his glasses off and folds them into his shirt pocket. Amara writes ship in the minutes.

Exactly right. A readiness review before shipping confirms, against criteria agreed with the receiver, that the system and everything going with it are ready to move, and that each open item has an owner, a plan and the receiver's agreement.

Wednesday of week thirty seven Ines, FRO's quality manager, brought the binder to Nadia's desk, all three inches of it, Wes's Product Development Process from the cargo days. The crewed programs tab from week one had grown fat. The design checklist's new line about single valves. Ines's own check that every verification point for a hazard control sits where the crew will be. The rest of what HEARTH had changed along the way was in HEARTH's own files, or in the heads of the people who'd done it.
The second module kicks off in three weeks, Ines said. Which of this do they open?
Most of what HEARTH learned isn't in Wes's binder. What should happen to it?
A. Fold HEARTH's changes into the binder through Wes, then check they're used.
B. Replace the binder with the handbook now that HEARTH has outgrown it.
C. Give the next program HEARTH's SEMP to start from, and leave the binder as it is.
D. Let the next team pick whatever it likes from HEARTH and the binder.

Wes and Ines go through it tab by tab. The crewed tab stops being a tab and becomes the binder. Every change HEARTH made goes in with its reason and Wes's name as owner, whether it started as a procedure or as somebody's habit, and the cargo steps that don't fit crewed work come out. Ines puts a check on the second module's first two reviews to see whether people follow the new pages, and why, if they don't.
That's the one. Life cycle model management sets up the organization's processes and models, assesses how they work, and improves them through their owner, then checks the change took.

Wednesday of week thirty eight Commander Tess Okonjo came back with Halo's two launch site technicians. The technicians would spend two days inside HEARTH with Gus and Tiago. Tess had asked for an hour.

She spent most of it in quarter four. Nadia found her sitting on the edge of the bunk under the new detector, looking at the photo. Then Tess worked the tape loose, slowly, so it wouldn't tear the corner, and put her boys in her chest pocket.
It's on your list, she said. Remove before flight. It goes up in my kit, and it goes back on that wall. She buttoned the pocket. Helen says you tested with it up.
Mallory came by at four with the acceptance certificate in a folder. I sign this on the dock Friday, and she's ours, he said. What else do I need?
Tess has her photo, and the certificate is ready to sign. How should FRO deliver HEARTH?
A. Keep title with FRO until launch, and HEARTH's risk with it until orbit.
B. Sign on the dock, with the acceptance test done and Halo's people taking over.
C. Hand it over with trained technicians, its data and a checkout at the far end.
D. Sign it on the dock, with the data package and procedures sent after it ships.

The certificate gets its package: the as-built record, the matrix with every row's evidence, the hazard reports, the procedures, the open items, and the limits Halo's controllers need to know. Halo's technicians spend two days doing every launch site task with their own hands. Title passes on the dock. The plan still has FRO and Halo repeating the leak and power checks at the launch site before HEARTH goes anywhere near the rocket.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Transition hands over a system able to work in its new environment: trained operators and maintainers, records and data, known limitations, and a checkout at the destination confirming it's ready for operation.

Thursday of week thirty eight Amara gave the lessons session the whole afternoon and the big room. Wes, Tiago, Jun, Odette, Ines, Gus, the harness lead, the flight software lead, and Helen on the screen. Pavel and Irena drove down from Frederick.

Nadia wrote the first one on the whiteboard herself: put verification points where the crew will be, not where the test will pass. Then they came fast. Name the interface control document in the purchase agreement. Ask a supplier what changed in its process, not only whether the part met spec. Every swap in troubleshooting gets a restore step. One valve. Put the crew in it before you call it done. By five there were thirty nine.

The second module's team was twenty people, most of them hired since spring, and four of them had been in the room. Tiago capped his marker. We've got a lessons folder, he said. It's got two hundred and fourteen documents in it. Want me to add one more?
Thirty nine lessons fill the whiteboard by five. How should FRO keep them for the second module?
A. Hold the lessons write-up until after launch, once the whole story is known.
B. Move HEARTH's best people onto the second module, with what they know.
C. Build each lesson into the new team's assets, with HEARTH's people paired in.
D. Write up today's lessons in one thorough report for the new team's first day.

Each of the thirty nine gets an owner and a home: a page in the binder, a check in the model, a step in a procedure, a line in the shared assets. Tess's twenty seven items go on the new module's needs list. Then the harder part. Every engineer on the new team is paired with someone from HEARTH through their first review, so what nobody wrote down gets passed along anyway.

Exactly right. Knowledge management captures lessons and know-how as reusable assets, puts them where future work meets them, and shares the knowledge that lives in experienced people through pairing and practice.

Friday of week thirty eight they rolled the big high bay doors open at ten at night, and the cold came in across the concrete. HEARTH sat on a low trailer in its container with a dry nitrogen line hissing into it and the recorders blinking on its side. Most of the four hundred had stayed. Some had brought their kids.

Amara climbed onto the Centennial Lighting crate. She didn't do the numbers this time. Nadia took the card out of her badge holder and handed it up, and Amara read it out loud. Six weeks late. Four people out. She turned it over. Her three conditions from the board vote were on the back in her own pen, and all three had held. She put it in her shirt pocket.
I told you six, she said. It's six. She got down. That was the speech.
On the dock Mallory uncapped his pen and looked past Amara, at her. Still ready? Still ready, Nadia said. He signed.
Wes rode in the escort truck. Before he climbed in he walked once around the container with his palm flat on its side, as he'd held it on the cell window during proof.

At ten to midnight the trailer pulled out under the old sign and its little space station sticker, and turned toward the airport at walking speed behind two police cars. A cargo plane big enough to swallow it was waiting there to take it to the coast.

Afterward the high bay was very big. Tiago's blue tape was still on the floor where he'd laid it down in week two, scuffed nearly white, with its two red X's. Next to it somebody had started a new rectangle in green tape, a little shorter. Three quarters.
Nadia stood in quarter four's square. Her father had stood there in week eleven with his left hand in his jacket pocket and called it the long way. She walked to the second red X. Three steps.
Tiago watched from the doorway with his coffee, the floor scraper leaning on the wall beside him. He left the blue tape for the morning.
In the car she texted Pueblo. Shipped. I'll be down tomorrow by noon.
A text from Dad. ILL MAKE EGGS
Twenty one months after that, HEARTH went up on a Thursday night in June, from the coast, on the heavy rocket it had always been meant for.

FRO threw a party in the high bay, with a taco truck in the lot and Amara up on the crate reading names, five hundred and some by then. Nadia watched from Pueblo. She'd asked Amara for the night back in January. Amara had said good, and go, and don't call me.

Her father had the stream on with the sound up, which he did for the Broncos and nothing else. Her sister Callie had the end of the couch, feet under her, a bag of pretzels in her lap. Rosie had Mom's chair by the window, and she didn't have to kneel on it anymore. The purple rocket was still on the fridge under the trout magnet from Salida, curled at the corners, the green door gone a little gray where somebody kept touching it.

At 7:52 the rocket went, so bright the TV made it a white smear with a stick under it. Her father said it looked like a cutting torch. Go ahead, Callie said, very quietly, in her radio voice, then looked surprised at herself and ate a pretzel.

Twenty minutes in, the stream put up a drawing of HEARTH, galley and quarters and two hatches. Rosie climbed off the chair, wedged herself in between Nadia and her grandfather, and studied it with her mouth open, pretzel salt on her chin. Where do the astronauts sleep?
Four beds, Nadia said, and leaned over and put a finger on the last one, right by the back door. The far quarter. I checked.
Rosie looked at the screen, then at the fridge, checking it against the green door, and seemed to find it all in order.

It took the upper stage about four hours to bring HEARTH up under the station. Rosie was out cold inside the first hour, against her grandfather, a finger hooked through his left hand like a mug handle. Callie made coffee and forgot it. The man on the stream said nominal about forty times. At ten to twelve, on the night side, the arm came down and took hold. Somewhere a man with a headset around his neck had found a target with nothing shiny within a meter of it. It took most of an hour to bring it in to the port, and a little before one the bolts went in, sixteen of them. Nadia counted.
A text from Helen. Berthed. All sixteen bolts. Leak check in the morning, then the node, then the crew. Tess says to tell you she's still keeping four.
Then the arm let go. On the TV its hand opened, slow, and drifted back a meter, then two, and HEARTH stayed put.

Her father didn't say anything for a long time. His sleeve was shoved up past the elbow. The TV lit the scar from his wrist nearly to the crook of his arm, shiny, pulled tight, and Rosie's finger was still hooked in the hand that didn't close. He hadn't moved it in four hours. Callie's head came down on Nadia's shoulder, heavy, half asleep.
I'd have climbed that one, he said, to the TV, the way he'd sign off on a crew's work.

Nobody went for the remote. The man on the stream said nominal again. The station went around into the night side with HEARTH bolted on the end of it, four beds made up and nobody in them yet, and Rosie kept her finger where it was the whole way around, ninety two minutes, Nadia timed it.
